title: Information exchange in an epilepsy forum on the World Wide Web
screen_reason: Content analysis of a sample of posts and responses on the MGH Neurology Epilepsy Webforum (March 1995 to February 1997). Responses were reviewed for objective accuracy by three epileptologists and an epilepsy nurse against published material, and the paper reports a share of items judged inaccurate with a denominator: 'Inaccurate statements of fact were present in 6% of the posts' (21 inaccurate responses). That is a CONTENT estimate judged against an external ground truth, not a quality-scale score.

estimates.country: Not stated for users; the forum is hosted by the Massachusetts General Hospital Neurology Service, Boston, USA, and the paper notes users are geographically dispersed
estimates.platform: MGH Neurology Epilepsy Webforum (unmoderated web bulletin board at neuro-www.mgh.harvard.edu/forum/)
estimates.measure_type: % of forum responses containing an objectively inaccurate statement of fact
estimates.value_raw: Inaccurate statements of fact were present in 6% of the posts; 21 inaccurate responses reviewed
estimates.denominator: The responses made to a systematic 1-in-7 sample of 155 primary posts to the epilepsy Webforum; the Results and abstract give 342 responses, the Methods section gives 372
estimates.definition: A statement of fact in a response that the review panel judged objectively inaccurate and that was confirmed as an error against appropriate published material; personal opinion and observations were excluded from the accuracy judgement
estimates.misinfo_def: We also reviewed the responses to the primary posts for objective accuracy. The responses were reviewed independently by three epileptologists and an epilepsy nurse. Only statements of fact were judged for accu- racy. Personal opinion and observations were not in- cludedinthisanalysis.
estimates.source_quote: Inaccurate statements of fact were present in 6% of the posts.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 32 (also Abstract: 'Six percent of the information was objectively inaccurate'; Discussion, p. 33: 'less than 6% of the answers to questions were objectively inaccurate')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Responses reviewed independently by three epileptologists and an epilepsy nurse; statements the panel judged to be in error were then checked against appropriate published material. No inter-rater agreement statistic reported and no rule stated for combining the four reviewers' judgements.
estimates.moderator_quote: We examined every seventh primary post, of the totalposts,givingusasamplesizeof155primaryposts and372associatedresponses.
estimates.notes: The denominator is internally inconsistent in the paper: the abstract and Results say 342 responses to the 155 sampled primary posts, the Methods say 372. 21/342 = 6.1% and 21/372 = 5.6%; the Discussion says 'less than 6%', which fits 372, while the Abstract and Results state 6%. The verbatim 6% is kept per R8; neither part/whole recomputation is used. Year 1996 is the midpoint of the stated March 1995 to February 1997 window, not a stated collection year. Country coded Global because the paper states users are geographically dispersed and never reports their nationality; the host institution is US. sampling_frame coded random_platform for the systematic every-seventh-post interval sample of the forum's full archive (a probability sample, not a keyword or curated set). The authors themselves note the figure is a lower bound: 'as we limited our scrutiny to statements of objective fact, the actual amount of misinformation, through implication or personal opinion, is undoubtedly greater.'

missed_or_uncertain: Considered and not extracted: (1) poster-type shares (care-givers 49%/42%, patients 34%/35%, health professionals <1%/2%, unidentified 16%/21% for primary posts; care-givers 34%, patients 38%, health professionals 6%, unidentified 22% for responses) — who posted, not whether the content was false; (2) post-type shares (80% questions, 13% announcements, 13% other) and the question-topic breakdown in Table 3 (treatment 31%, natural history 28%, shared experiences 20%, side effects 18%) — topical composition, not falsity; (3) '20% of the questions' where users remarked a health-care provider had not met their information needs — dissatisfaction, not misinformation; (4) 'about 6% of the primary posts were clearly responses rather than initiators' — a data-cleaning figure, coincidentally also 6%, and unrelated to accuracy; (5) 'Only 6% of the discussants identified themselves as health-care providers' — expertise composition. I did not split the 6% by poster type (6 care-givers, 9 patients, 1 health professional, 5 unidentified of 21) because the paper gives no per-group denominators, so any such share would be an invented sub-row. rob.design: Retrospective content analysis of one unmoderated disease-specific web forum. Frame: all primary posts and linked responses to the MGH Neurology Epilepsy Webforum between March 1995 and February 1997 (the Epilepsy Forum was 12.8% of the 3,881 total posts across the 40 neurology forums); every seventh primary post was drawn, yielding 155 primary posts and their associated responses. 'Orphaned' posts (about 6%) that were responses misfiled as primary posts were excluded. Accuracy coding: responses reviewed independently by three epileptologists and an epilepsy nurse; only statements of fact were judged; suspected errors were verified against published material. No inter-rater reliability statistic, no adjudication rule, and no coding manual are reported. Denominator for the accuracy rate is reported inconsistently (342 vs 372 responses).
